cards.title: GKE Standard — Managed Kubernetes with Node Control
cards.teaser: GKE Standard gives you a Google-managed Kubernetes control plane while you retain full control over node configuration, OS images, machine types, and cluster autoscaling behavior. It is the right choice when you need to tune the runtime environment.

runs.text: Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) Standard is GCP's managed Kubernetes offering where Google operates the control plane (API server, etcd, scheduler, controller manager) at no extra charge, but you provision and manage the worker nodes.
Creating a Standard cluster with gcloud:

explanation.text:
gcloud container clusters create my-cluster \
  --region us-central1 \
  --machine-type e2-standard-4 \
  --num-nodes 3 \
  --enable-autoscaling \
  --min-nodes 1 \
  --max-nodes 10 \
  --workload-pool my-project.svc.id.goog \
  --release-channel regular

runs.text: Key knobs available only in Standard:

items.text: — swap the default Container-Optimized OS for Ubuntu or use shielded VMs.
— useful for kernel tuning, eBPF-based tools, and hardware drivers (GPUs, TPUs).
— compliance scenarios that require dedicated physical hardware.
— advanced runtime configuration not exposed in Autopilot.

runs.text: You pay for the VMs whether or not pods are running on them, so right-sizing node pools and enabling cluster autoscaler is essential. The
--release-channel
flag (rapid / regular / stable) controls how quickly GKE auto-upgrades your nodes to newer Kubernetes versions.

GKE automatically applies security patches to the control plane. For nodes, automatic upgrades are enabled by default on most channels. Disabling them is possible but means you own the patching burden.
GKE Standard: Google runs the Kubernetes brain, you run the worker machines. You get full control over what those machines look like, but you also have to pay for them and keep them right-sized.

cards.title: GKE Autopilot — Nodes Abstracted Away
cards.teaser: GKE Autopilot removes the node entirely from your operational model. Google provisions, scales, and patches the underlying infrastructure; you declare pods and pay per pod-second of vCPU and memory consumed.

runs.text: Autopilot flips the GKE billing and ops model: instead of managing VMs that may or may not be fully utilized, you describe what your workloads need and Google handles everything below the pod boundary.
Creating an Autopilot cluster:

explanation.text:
gcloud container clusters create-auto my-autopilot-cluster \
  --region us-central1 \
  --workload-pool my-project.svc.id.goog

runs.text: GKE Standard vs Autopilot — the comparison that matters:

items.text: — Standard: you manage node pools. Autopilot: Google manages nodes entirely; they are invisible.
— Standard: pay for VMs (even idle capacity). Autopilot: pay per pod CPU/memory request; no charge for idle node headroom.
— Standard: privileged containers and DaemonSets are allowed. Autopilot: privileged mode is blocked; DaemonSets are restricted.
— Standard: Cluster Autoscaler adjusts node count. Autopilot: instantaneous, no node warm-up visible to the user.
— Standard: workloads needing kernel access, GPUs, or custom node images. Autopilot: stateless microservices, batch jobs, most production web APIs.

runs.text: Autopilot enforces resource requests on every container — pods without requests are rejected at admission. This is a feature: it forces capacity planning to be explicit and makes billing predictable.

Autopilot does not support DaemonSets in the traditional sense. If your tooling (logging agents, security scanners) relies on DaemonSets with host-level access, you need Standard or must migrate to sidecar-based approaches.
GKE Autopilot: tell Kubernetes what your pods need, Google figures out what machines to run them on, and you only pay for what your pods actually use. No nodes to babysit.

cards.title: Node Pools — Heterogeneous Worker Groups
cards.teaser: A GKE Standard cluster can contain multiple node pools, each with a different machine type, OS image, or GPU configuration. Node pools let you run diverse workloads in one cluster without forcing every pod to accept the same hardware.

runs.text: A node pool is a group of VMs within a GKE cluster that share the same configuration. Every cluster starts with a default node pool, but you can add as many additional pools as needed.
Adding a GPU node pool to an existing cluster:

explanation.text:
gcloud container node-pools create gpu-pool \
  --cluster my-cluster \
  --region us-central1 \
  --machine-type n1-standard-8 \
  --accelerator type=nvidia-tesla-t4,count=1 \
  --num-nodes 2 \
  --node-taints nvidia.com/gpu=present:NoSchedule

runs.text: Common node pool patterns:

items.text: — e2-standard-4 or n2-standard-8 for most web services and APIs.
— m2-ultramem-* for in-memory caches or Java services with large heaps.
for batch workloads; up to 80% cost reduction at the cost of eviction risk.
— for .NET Framework workloads that require a Windows container runtime.

runs.text: Pods are directed to the right pool via node selectors, node affinity rules, or taints and tolerations. A taint on the GPU pool (
nvidia.com/gpu=present:NoSchedule
) prevents non-GPU pods from landing there accidentally.
Each node pool has its own autoscaling configuration. You can set a spot pool to scale from 0 to 100 for burst batch work while keeping your general-purpose pool stable at 3–10 nodes.

Node pools are like different sections in a warehouse — each section has the right shelving and equipment for its contents. You use taints and labels to route pods to the pool that has the hardware they need.

cards.title: Artifact Registry — Container and Package Storage
cards.teaser: Artifact Registry is GCP's unified private repository for container images, Helm charts, Maven artifacts, npm packages, and Python wheels. It replaced the older Container Registry (gcr.io) in 2023 and Container Registry was fully deprecated by 2024.

runs.text: Artifact Registry lives at
REGION-docker.pkg.dev/PROJECT/REPO/IMAGE:TAG
and is tightly integrated with GCP IAM, VPC Service Controls, and Cloud Build.
Creating a Docker repository and pushing an image:

explanation.text:
# Create the repository
gcloud artifacts repositories create my-repo \
  --repository-format docker \
  --location us-central1 \
  --description "Production container images"

# Configure Docker to authenticate with Artifact Registry
gcloud auth configure-docker us-central1-docker.pkg.dev

# Tag and push
docker tag my-app:latest \
  us-central1-docker.pkg.dev/my-project/my-repo/my-app:latest
docker push us-central1-docker.pkg.dev/my-project/my-repo/my-app:latest

runs.text: Key advantages over the deprecated Container Registry (gcr.io):

items.text: — one registry for Docker images, Helm charts, Maven JARs, npm packages, and Python wheels.
— fine-grained permissions per repository, not just per project.
— on-push scanning with Artifact Analysis (formerly Container Analysis); results visible in the GCP console.
— encrypt stored artifacts with customer-managed Cloud KMS keys.
— store images close to the clusters that pull them to reduce latency and egress costs.

runs.text: Container Registry (gcr.io) was deprecated in 2023 and shut down for new projects in 2024. All new repositories should use Artifact Registry. Existing gcr.io images can be migrated with gcloud artifacts docker upgrade.

Artifact Registry is GCP's private package warehouse — it stores your container images (and Helm charts, Maven JARs, npm packages) with IAM access control and built-in vulnerability scanning. It replaced the older gcr.io Container Registry.

cards.title: Cloud Build — GCP's Native CI for Containers
cards.teaser: Cloud Build is a fully managed CI service that executes build steps in containers, natively integrates with Artifact Registry and GKE, and produces provenance attestations for supply-chain security — all without managing build infrastructure.

runs.text: Cloud Build runs each build step inside a Docker container, which means every tool in the ecosystem is available — just reference the image. There are no agents to patch or queues to scale.
A minimal
cloudbuild.yaml
that builds, tests, and pushes to Artifact Registry:

explanation.text:
steps:
  - name: 'gcr.io/cloud-builders/docker'
    args:
      - build
      - '-t'
      - 'us-central1-docker.pkg.dev/$PROJECT_ID/my-repo/my-app:$COMMIT_SHA'
      - '.'

  - name: 'gcr.io/cloud-builders/docker'
    args:
      - run
      - '--rm'
      - 'us-central1-docker.pkg.dev/$PROJECT_ID/my-repo/my-app:$COMMIT_SHA'
      - 'pytest'

  - name: 'gcr.io/cloud-builders/docker'
    args:
      - push
      - 'us-central1-docker.pkg.dev/$PROJECT_ID/my-repo/my-app:$COMMIT_SHA'

images:
  - 'us-central1-docker.pkg.dev/$PROJECT_ID/my-repo/my-app:$COMMIT_SHA'

options:
  logging: CLOUD_LOGGING_ONLY

runs.text: Cloud Build features relevant for GKE workflows:

items.text: — connect to GitHub, GitLab, or Cloud Source Repositories; fire on push, PR, or tag.
— Cloud Build can generate SLSA Level 3 provenance automatically, which Binary Authorization can verify before allowing a deployment.
— run builds inside your VPC for access to private resources like internal registries or databases.

runs.text: Cloud Build's service account needs the Artifact Registry Writer role to push images and the GKE Developer role to deploy. Granting least-privilege roles to the build SA is a prerequisite for supply-chain security.
Cloud Build is GCP's managed CI: you describe build steps in YAML, each step runs in a container, and the output (your image) lands straight in Artifact Registry. No CI servers to run.

cards.title: GKE Workload Identity — Pod to GCP Service Account Mapping
cards.teaser: Workload Identity is the secure, supported way to grant GKE pods access to GCP APIs. It replaces the fragile metadata-server workarounds and node-SA key files by binding a Kubernetes ServiceAccount directly to a GCP IAM service account.

runs.text: Before Workload Identity, pods that needed GCP API access either relied on the node's service account (over-privileged), used mounted key JSON files (fragile, secret management nightmare), or intercepted the metadata server (complex, error-prone).

Workload Identity works through a two-way binding: the Kubernetes ServiceAccount (KSA) is annotated with the GCP Service Account (GSA) email, and the GSA is granted permission to impersonate itself via the KSA identity.
Step 1 — Enable the workload pool on the cluster (included in the create command earlier via
--workload-pool
). Step 2 — Create the IAM binding:

explanation.text:
# Create a GCP service account
gcloud iam service-accounts create my-app-sa \
  --project my-project

# Grant it the permissions it needs (example: read from a GCS bucket)
gcloud projects add-iam-policy-binding my-project \
  --member serviceAccount:my-app-sa@my-project.iam.gserviceaccount.com \
  --role roles/storage.objectViewer

# Allow the KSA to impersonate the GSA
gcloud iam service-accounts add-iam-policy-binding \
  my-app-sa@my-project.iam.gserviceaccount.com \
  --role roles/iam.workloadIdentityUser \
  --member "serviceAccount:my-project.svc.id.goog[my-namespace/my-ksa]"

runs.text: Step 3 — Annotate the Kubernetes ServiceAccount:

explanation.text:
apiVersion: v1
kind: ServiceAccount
metadata:
  name: my-ksa
  namespace: my-namespace
  annotations:
    iam.gke.io/gcp-service-account: my-app-sa@my-project.iam.gserviceaccount.com

runs.text: Pods using
serviceAccountName: my-ksa
automatically receive short-lived tokens through the GKE metadata server. No JSON key file is ever placed on disk.
Workload Identity requires the workload-pool feature to be enabled at cluster creation. Enabling it after the fact requires a node pool recreation. Plan for it from the start.

Workload Identity is a trust handshake: you tell GCP "this Kubernetes service account speaks for that GCP service account," so pods get GCP credentials automatically without storing any keys anywhere.

cards.title: Binary Authorization — Admission-Time Image Policy
cards.teaser: Binary Authorization is a GKE admission controller that blocks deployment of container images that do not carry a valid cryptographic attestation. It enforces the principle that only images that passed specific checks — build, scan, sign — can run in production.

runs.text: Binary Authorization (BinAuthz) sits between the Kubernetes API server and the kubelet. When a pod is admitted, BinAuthz inspects the container image digest and requires that one or more
attestors
have signed off on that exact digest.
The policy lifecycle:

items.text: — a named authority (e.g., "CI-passed", "security-scanned") backed by a Cloud KMS asymmetric key pair.
— a signed note in Artifact Analysis that says attestor X vouches for image digest Y. Cloud Build can generate these automatically.
— a YAML or JSON document defining which attestors are required for each cluster or namespace, and what happens when a check fails (allow, deny, warn).

explanation.text:
# Example BinAuthz policy requiring both attestors
globalPolicyEvaluationMode: REQUIRE_ATTESTATION
defaultAdmissionRule:
  evaluationMode: REQUIRE_ATTESTATION
  enforcementMode: ENFORCED_BLOCK_AND_AUDIT_LOG
  requireAttestationsBy:
    - projects/my-project/attestors/cloud-build-attestor
    - projects/my-project/attestors/vulnerability-scan-attestor

runs.text: Binary Authorization integrates with Cloud Build provenance (SLSA) so that images built by your Cloud Build pipeline automatically carry the build attestation. Combined with a vulnerability scan attestor, you get a two-factor gate before any image reaches a GKE cluster.

BinAuthz operates on image digests (sha256 hashes), not tags. A tag can be repointed; a digest cannot. This prevents tag mutation attacks where a malicious image replaces a trusted one behind the same tag.

Binary Authorization is a bouncer at the GKE door: before any container image is allowed to run, it checks for signed certificates from trusted authorities (your CI pipeline, your security scanner). No signature, no entry.

cards.title: GKE Security Posture — Vulnerability Scanning and Runtime Security
cards.teaser: GKE Security Posture is a built-in dashboard and scanning engine that provides continuous visibility into workload vulnerabilities, OS-level CVEs, and runtime anomalies across your clusters — without requiring a separate security agent.

runs.text: Enabling GKE Security Posture:

explanation.text:
gcloud container clusters update my-cluster \
  --region us-central1 \
  --enable-workload-vulnerability-scanning \
  --security-posture standard

runs.text: GKE Security Posture surfaces three categories of findings in the Security tab of the GKE console:

items.text: — continuous scanning of running container images for OS-level CVEs using Artifact Analysis. Findings are tied to the specific workload and namespace, not just the image.
— flags misconfigurations like pods running as root, containers with dangerous capabilities, or missing resource limits.
— detects anomalous in-cluster behaviors such as unexpected reverse shells, crypto mining activity, or lateral movement, powered by eBPF-based syscall monitoring.

runs.text: The security posture integrates with Cloud Security Command Center (SCC) for centralized finding management across projects. Severity levels (Critical, High, Medium, Low) align with CVSS scores.

GKE Security Posture is available in Standard and Autopilot clusters. The Advanced tier (which includes runtime threat detection) is part of GKE Enterprise. The standard tier vulnerability scanning is available on all cluster types at no additional charge.

GKE Security Posture is a continuous health monitor for your cluster: it scans your running containers for known CVEs, checks your workload configs for risky settings, and in the premium tier watches for suspicious runtime behavior.

cards.title: GKE Multi-Cluster Ingress — Global Load Balancing Across Clusters
cards.teaser: GKE Multi-Cluster Ingress (MCI) is a GKE-native resource that provisions a single Google Cloud external HTTP(S) load balancer with backends spread across multiple GKE clusters in multiple regions, giving you global traffic distribution with a single IP.

runs.text: Standard Kubernetes Ingress creates a regional load balancer. Multi-Cluster Ingress elevates this to a single global Cloud Load Balancer that routes user traffic to the nearest healthy cluster.
MCI requires GKE Hub (fleet) and a config cluster — one designated cluster that holds the
MultiClusterIngress
and
MultiClusterService
resources:

explanation.text:
# MultiClusterService selects pods from all member clusters
apiVersion: networking.gke.io/v1
kind: MultiClusterService
metadata:
  name: my-app-mcs
  namespace: my-namespace
spec:
  template:
    spec:
      selector:
        app: my-app
      ports:
        - name: http
          protocol: TCP
          port: 8080
---
# MultiClusterIngress binds the global LB to the MCS
apiVersion: networking.gke.io/v1
kind: MultiClusterIngress
metadata:
  name: my-app-mci
  namespace: my-namespace
spec:
  template:
    spec:
      backend:
        serviceName: my-app-mcs
        servicePort: 8080

runs.text: Traffic behavior:

items.text: — a single global IP; Google's network routes each user to the closest healthy backend cluster.
— if a cluster's pods fail health checks, traffic automatically shifts to other member clusters.
— shift traffic percentage between clusters for gradual multi-region rollouts.

runs.text: MCI requires all member clusters to be registered to the same GKE Hub fleet. Fleet registration is the prerequisite for all Anthos multi-cluster features, including Config Sync and Service Mesh.
Multi-Cluster Ingress puts a single global load balancer in front of multiple GKE clusters across regions. Users hit one IP and get routed to the nearest healthy cluster automatically.

cards.title: Anthos — Multi-Cluster, Hybrid, and Multi-Cloud Management
cards.teaser: Anthos is Google's platform for managing fleets of Kubernetes clusters regardless of where they run — GKE on GCP, GKE on AWS (GKE Multi-Cloud), on-premises (GKE on Bare Metal / VMware), or attached third-party clusters. The unifying primitive is the GKE Hub fleet.

runs.text: Anthos is not a single product — it is a bundle of capabilities applied consistently across a fleet of clusters. The fleet is the logical grouping; each cluster is registered as a fleet member via GKE Hub.
The core Anthos components:

items.text: — registers clusters from any environment into a single fleet; enables cross-cluster features.
— GitOps controller that synchronizes Kubernetes manifests from a Git repository to all fleet clusters.
— managed Istio control plane for mTLS, traffic management, and observability across the fleet.
— OPA Gatekeeper-based admission controller for enforcing policy as code (resource limits, label requirements, allowed registries).
— global load balancing across fleet clusters (covered in the previous card).

runs.text: Registering an external cluster to a fleet:

explanation.text:
gcloud container fleet memberships register my-onprem-cluster \
  --project my-project \
  --context on-prem-cluster-context \
  --service-account-key-file /path/to/sa-key.json

runs.text: Once registered, the cluster can receive Config Sync, Policy Controller, and ASM configurations from the fleet hub, achieving uniform policy and configuration management across GCP and non-GCP environments.

Anthos was rebranded as part of GKE Enterprise in 2023. The underlying components (Config Sync, ASM, Policy Controller) are still called by their component names in the GCP documentation and gcloud commands.

Anthos is the control plane that sits above all your Kubernetes clusters, wherever they live. You register every cluster — GCP, AWS, on-prem — into one fleet, then push config, policy, and service mesh configuration to all of them from one place.

cards.title: Config Sync — Anthos GitOps Controller
cards.teaser: Config Sync is the Anthos component that continuously reconciles the state of a Kubernetes cluster (or an entire fleet) with the desired state declared in a Git repository. It is the GitOps engine at the heart of Anthos configuration management.

runs.text: Config Sync runs as a set of controllers inside the cluster. It watches a Git repository (or OCI artifact source) and applies any changes to the cluster automatically, providing the core GitOps guarantee: the cluster always converges to what is in Git.
Enabling Config Sync on a fleet:

explanation.text:
gcloud beta container fleet config-management enable \
  --project my-project

runs.text: Configuring a cluster to sync from a repository:

explanation.text:
# ConfigManagement resource applied to the cluster
apiVersion: configmanagement.gke.io/v1
kind: ConfigManagement
metadata:
  name: config-management
spec:
  configSync:
    enabled: true
    sourceFormat: unstructured
    git:
      syncRepo: https://github.com/my-org/my-fleet-config
      syncBranch: main
      secretType: gcpserviceaccount
      gcpServiceAccountEmail: config-sync-sa@my-project.iam.gserviceaccount.com

runs.text: Config Sync capabilities:

items.text: — cluster-scoped and namespace-scoped resources can be organized in a hierarchy; child namespaces inherit policies from parent nodes.
— if a resource is modified directly on the cluster (kubectl apply without going through Git), Config Sync detects and reverts the drift.
— sync from an OCI image stored in Artifact Registry instead of Git, enabling signed and versioned config bundles.
— apply a config change to all registered clusters simultaneously or roll it out progressively by cluster group.

runs.text: Config Sync can coexist with ArgoCD or Flux. Some teams use Config Sync for cluster-wide infrastructure policies (RBAC, network policies, namespaces) and ArgoCD for application-level GitOps, with clear ownership boundaries between them.
Config Sync watches your Git repo and keeps your cluster in sync with it. If someone changes something directly on the cluster, Config Sync notices and revertes it back to what Git says it should be.

cards.title: GKE Enterprise — Premium Tier with Mesh, Multi-Cluster, and Advanced Features
cards.teaser: GKE Enterprise (formerly Anthos) is the premium GKE licensing tier that bundles Anthos Service Mesh, Config Sync, Policy Controller, multi-cluster ingress, fleet management, and advanced security features under a per-vCPU pricing model.

runs.text: In 2023, Google unified the Anthos brand under GKE Enterprise. The distinction is now: GKE Standard and Autopilot are the base clusters; GKE Enterprise is the premium management layer applied on top of those clusters.
What GKE Enterprise adds over base GKE:

items.text: — Google-managed Istio with automatic certificate rotation, traffic management, and distributed tracing across the fleet.
— fleet-wide GitOps and OPA-based policy enforcement included in the Enterprise license.
— global load balancing across clusters (Enterprise feature; not available in base GKE).
— runtime threat detection (eBPF-based), compliance dashboards, and additional audit logging.
— GKE Multi-Cloud (running GKE on AWS or Azure) and GKE on Bare Metal / VMware are Enterprise features.
— 99.95% cluster control plane SLA vs 99.5% for base GKE Standard.

runs.text: GKE Enterprise is billed per vCPU per hour across all fleet-registered clusters, including non-GCP ones. This makes the cost predictable and tied to workload size rather than a flat per-cluster fee.

If your architecture needs service mesh, multi-cluster ingress, or hybrid/multi-cloud management, GKE Enterprise is the supported path. Trying to bolt Istio and ArgoCD onto base GKE for these scenarios is possible but unsupported and operationally heavier.

GKE Enterprise is the upgrade tier: take your GKE clusters, register them in a fleet, and unlock service mesh, GitOps config management, global load balancing, and hybrid-cloud support — all managed by Google and billed per vCPU.

cards.title: Cloud Run on GKE — Knative-Based Serverless on Kubernetes
cards.teaser: Cloud Run for Anthos (now called Cloud Run on GKE) brought the Cloud Run developer experience — deploy a container, GCP handles scaling — to clusters you own. It is built on Knative Serving and lets you run event-driven, scale-to-zero workloads inside GKE.

runs.text: Cloud Run exists in two forms on GCP:

items.text: — Google manages the underlying infrastructure entirely; you just push a container. This is the standard Cloud Run product and the recommended default for stateless serverless workloads.

— runs the same Knative Serving runtime inside your GKE cluster. You get Cloud Run's developer experience (scale to zero, event triggers, HTTP-based routing) on infrastructure you control, including access to private network resources.

runs.text: Knative Serving, the underlying technology, provides:

items.text: — each deployment creates an immutable revision; traffic can be split between revisions for canary releases.
— the Knative autoscaler scales pods down to zero when there is no traffic; they scale back up on the first request (cold start latency applies).
— Pub/Sub, Cloud Storage, and custom event sources can trigger service invocations without direct HTTP calls.

runs.text: Why use Cloud Run on GKE instead of fully managed Cloud Run?

items.text: — the workload runs inside your cluster and can reach private databases, internal APIs, and on-premises resources via VPN.
— GPU-accelerated ML inference workloads that need scale-to-zero but also need GPU node pools.
— regulated workloads that must run in customer-controlled infrastructure, not Google's shared serverless fleet.

runs.text: Cloud Run for Anthos was the original branding. As of 2024, the feature is available under GKE Enterprise via the Knative add-on. For new projects, evaluate fully managed Cloud Run first; Cloud Run on GKE adds operational complexity that is only justified by the private network or compliance requirements above.

Cloud Run on GKE brings the serverless developer experience — deploy a container, it scales itself to zero when idle — into a GKE cluster you control. It is built on Knative and is useful when you need scale-to-zero but also need to stay inside your own VPC.
